newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU's Brittan says full new trade round vital.
newsitem.headline: EU's Brittan says full new trade round vital.

text.p: Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, pushing against U.S. objections, on Tuesday issued a ringing plea for the launch of a new round of global trade negotiations at the turn of the century.

Brittan, in a speech setting out the Brussels agenda for liberalisation in the booming world services sector, also urged emerging economies to come up quickly with strong proposals for opening up their financial industries to outside firms.

"Services are a growth sector for all WTO (World Trade Organisation) member-countries, but services activities are mainly a big earner for developed countries," he told a Geneva conference of global service industry groupings.
"In these circumstances, a big package of liberalisation for services is likely only to be achieved if the services negotiation is part of an even broader process," Brittan said.
"That is why we need a new global round of trade liberalisation," he declared.

Brittan has already put up the idea of what he has dubbed a "Millenium Round", which would be the eighth of its type since a world trading system was set up in 1948 under the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT).

But he was clearly using the conference, attended by key service industry leaders from around the globe, in a bid to garner support from a sector widely seen as likely to provide the main base for the world economy in the 21st century.

The United States has shown little enthusiasm for a new round -- a set of negotiations ranging across the whole aspect of world trade from manufactured goods through farm produce to tourism and rights to patents.

The last such effort, the Uruguay Round, lasted from 1986 to the end of 1993 after running two years over its deadline, but produced accords on major tariff cuts and tougher rules trading states committed themselves to observe.

It also created the Geneva-based WTO, which now has a membership of 131 with nearly 30 other countries seeking entry. The trade body administers the system and its dispute settlement procedure which aims to enforce the rules.

Supporters of the "round" concept argue it allows for essential trade-offs where countries facing what they see as unfavourable accords in one sector can set potential losses against gains in other, often totally unrelated, areas.
Opponents say it makes reaching any agreements increasingly complicated as failure in one sector can lead to an entire package unravelling -- as almost happened in the Uruguay Round.

But in his Tuesday speech, Sir Leon said it would be over- optimistic to expect emerging economies to make a political effort for more liberalisation in an already agreed new set of service negotiations under the WTO due to start in the year 2000, without psospect of a trade-off.

Many of these countries had not yet established their "home-grown players" in services and were unlikely to open up unless the major industrial markets were to open more to their industrial or farm exports.

At the same time, in a clear appeal to developing countries, Brittan said all WTO members involved in current talks aimed at producing a pact on financial services by the year end should make "substantial contributions" by a July 15 deadline.
The United States and the EU have promised new offers of their own by that time and the other two top trading powers -- Japan and Canada -- have signalled they will follow.

But Sir Leon, echoing comments by U.S. officials at the last round of the talks earlier this month, said the sum total of offers now on the table was not enough for an accord and warned an interim agreement in 1995 could not be renewed.
